newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese, Japanese nationalism tangle in sticky row.
newsitem.headline: Chinese, Japanese nationalism tangle in sticky row.

text.p: Chinese nationalist fervour over a group of East China Sea islets is posing a tough dilemma for Japan, China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, all anxious to prevent the movement boiling into a frenzy that could rock the region.

A two-month-old campaign among Chinese communities across East Asia suffered its first casualty last week when Hong Kong activist David Chan drowned after jumping off a protest ship in defiance of a Japanese blockade of the islands.
Anger, shock and grief shook Hong Kong, where many debated whether Chan died as a martyr or as a fool, but protesters vowed to send a new protest flotilla to the islands.
"We should not give up until we have reclaimed the islands," said Chan's grieving sister Chan Lai-ying.

Others noted pathos and irony in Chan's death -- a "safety" rope that may have killed him by dragging him against the ship, the apology of a sobbing skipper who felt he was partly to blame, and the awkward fact that it was a Japanese medical team that tried to save Chan and did in fact save the life of a co-protester who also jumped in the sea.
Some analysts speculated whether similar hothead protests could stir unrest when Britain hands Hong Kong to China in 1997.

The uninhabited rocky outcrops in the East China Sea have kindled fiery passions among Chinese communities in Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and Macau since Japanese rightwing extremists built a lighthouse and planted flags there in July.
Tokyo has claimed sovereign rights to the islands, known by Japan as the Senkakus and by China as the Diaoyus, since 1895.
China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries. Taiwan also lays claim to the territory.
The governments affected have tried to calm the passions of the protest movement. Neither Beijing nor Tokyo want to spoil a vital economic relationship. Hong Kong has similar worries.
"I understand the depth of feeling but I hope views will be expressed in a calm manner without affecting the relationship between ourselves and Japan," Chief Secretary Anson Chan said.
Britain's colonial governor Chris Patten and China's chief official in Hong Kong, Zhou Nan, usually at loggerheads, were for once in harmony, expressing their sadness and condolences.
Officials in China expect the row to evaporate.
"We want to put this behind us," said one. "I don't think we are going to see this lead to anything serious. That would be in no one's best interests."
Diplomats said Beijing was anxious not to see things spiral out of control when its rival is a major trade partner.

But, while China had stifled protests on the mainland, it did not want to be seen as lukewarm on a territorial issue on which Beijing believed it had right on its side. China and Japan wanted an amicable solution, but were in no hurry.
In Tokyo, Japanese analysts said the issue was emotional rather than diplomatic, and that the anger of people in Taiwan, Hong Kong and China differed.
They said Taiwan's aim was independence, while Hong Kong's behaviour was conditioned by its return to Chinese rule in 1997.
"Hong Kong is angry at both Japan and China," said one Japanese analyst. "It may take until the reversion in 1997 for their anger to die down," he said.
"The pro-democrats will lose their identity if they keep on being anti-China, so they're using this case to show they're pro-democracy as well as Chinese," analyst Yoichi Masuzoe said.

"A lot of these activities reflect the impotence of the Chinese government in protecting sovereignty and whether that would be translated to a growing annoyance with the Chinese government," politics professor Peter Cheung told Reuters.
"Possibly, this is the intention of those participating in this movement," Cheung, from Hong Kong University, said.

The Taiwan government kept a low profile, urging calm, but editorials there demanded tough action. "We hope that after the sacrifice of David Chan", the popular United Daily News said, governments can "launch more aggressive actions".
